title: Have mercy on me (Psalm 50 [51])
hookLine: David's psalm after his great sin, prayed every Friday morning

cards: A prophet named Nathan walks into the king's palace with a story. Two men lived in a town, he says. One was rich, with flocks and herds.
The other was poor, with one little ewe lamb he raised with his children; it ate from his plate and slept in his arms.
When a traveler visited, the rich man spared his own sheep, took the poor man's lamb and served it for dinner. King David is furious. That man deserves to die, he says.
And Nathan looks at him and says four words.

teach.b: "Thou art the man." David had taken another man's wife, Bathsheba, and when she was pregnant, he arranged for her husband Uriah to die in battle. He thought it was hidden.
Now it's out. David, a king who could have had the prophet killed, says, "I have sinned against the Lord." The heading of Psalm 50 in the Douay, 51 in most Bibles, ties it to this moment.
Its Latin first word names it: Miserere, have mercy. "Have mercy on me, O God, according to thy great mercy." Nothing held back.
It asks to be washed: "Thou shalt sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed: thou shalt wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow."
Hyssop, a small plant, sprinkled water in purification rites; that verse is why a priest sprinkling holy water over a congregation is traditionally called the Asperges, from its Latin.

The center: "Create a clean heart in me, O God: and renew a right spirit within my bowels." Create is the Hebrew verb Genesis opens with, and scholars note the Bible uses it only of God. Not a cleaned-up heart: a new one.
Near the end, God doesn't want a burnt offering: "a contrite and humbled heart, O God, thou wilt not despise."
The Church prays this psalm every Friday morning in the Liturgy of the Hours, the day Jesus died.
It's also behind Allegri's Miserere, said to have been so guarded by the Sistine Chapel that copies were forbidden, until the young Mozart, the story goes, heard it and wrote it down from memory.

how: Catholics who pray the Liturgy of the Hours say the Miserere every Friday at Morning Prayer; it is one of the seven penitential psalms, and its verse about hyssop gave its name to the Asperges, the sprinkling with holy water.

games.q: you're King David. a prophet has just told you, thou art the man. you could have him thrown out, or worse. what do you do?
o: deny it and send him away.
say, I have sinned against the Lord.

games.why: David says, I have sinned against the Lord. the psalm's heading ties the Miserere to this moment.

practice: Let the psalm's first line be the only thing in your mind, slowly, once on each out-breath: have mercy on me, O God, according to thy great mercy. Don't go looking for your worst sin; let the line find whatever needs it.
If you pray, stay with those words to God; if you don't, breathe the word mercy, for yourself and someone you find it hard to forgive.

wordCard.voice: Miserere. Latin for have mercy, the first word and the name of David's psalm after his great sin. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: have mercy on me, O God, the psalm's first words in the Vulgate.

carryVoice: Your line: a clean heart. The psalm starts with mercy, not with excuses. See you tomorrow.
